items.def: Your urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising carbon dioxide, sensed by chemoreceptors in the brainstem. CO₂ also regulates blood pH and helps oxygen release from hemoglobin into your tissues (the Bohr effect). This is why 'more air' is not always 'more oxygen' — and why breathing less, at rest, can deliver more.
is the signal that tells you to breathe — not oxygen

Module 2 · The Science of Breath

Your heart doesn't tick like a metronome. The tiny, constant variation between beats reflects a responsive vagus nerve and a flexible autonomic system. Higher HRV is broadly associated with better stress resilience, recovery, and cardiovascular health. Slow breathing is one of the fastest ways to raise it in the moment.
the variation in time between heartbeats — higher is generally healthier

Bigger oscillations mean a stronger, better-exercised vagal brake.
This is measurable — many wearables let clients see it change.

sections.heading: The Risk Mindset: First, Do No Harm

items.def: Intensity ≠ safety   The stronger the practice, the greater the screening and care required.
Functional is gentle   Slow, light breathing is safe for nearly everyone.
Expansive is potent   Fast, sustained over-breathing needs real caution and screening.

items.text: Gentle · safe for nearly all
Strong · screen carefully

items.text: As you move right, the need for screening, skill, and caution rises with the intensity.

items.def: Heart & vascular   Heart disease, prior heart attack, uncontrolled high blood pressure, aneurysm.
Respiratory   Asthma or COPD — caution; keep inhaler close; avoid strong over-breathing.
Eyes & pressure   Glaucoma or detached retina — raised pressure is a risk.
Structural   Recent surgery or injury, severe osteoporosis; epilepsy noted next.
Module 5 · Safety, Ethics & Trauma-Informed Practice
Epilepsy / seizures   Over-breathing can lower the seizure threshold — avoid strong work.
Psychosis, schizophrenia, bipolar   Altered states can destabilize — avoid; refer to specialists.
Severe unprocessed trauma / PTSD   Needs trauma-specialist facilitation, gentle and titrated.
Panic disorder   Over-breathing mimics panic — start very gently, if at all.

A simple path to run for every prospective client before strong work:

items.text: Complete the intake   Written health form plus a real conversation.

items.def: Any red-flag condition?   Cardiac, epilepsy, psychiatric, pregnancy, trauma, etc.
If yes → gentle only or refer   Offer functional work, seek clearance, or refer out.
If no → proceed, still start gentle   Begin low, watch closely, earn intensity.
When in doubt, choose the gentler option, get medical clearance, or refer.
